title: Total Spread of All Subarrays
statement:
The spread of a block of numbers is its largest value minus its smallest value. You get an integer array nums.

Return the sum of the spreads of all contiguous non-empty subarrays of nums. A subarray of one value has spread 0. Two subarrays at different positions count separately even if they hold the same values.

examples.why: Single values give 0. [3, 1] gives 2, [1, 2] gives 1, [3, 1, 2] gives 2.
Every subarray has the same largest and smallest value.
[2, -1] gives 3, [-1, 4] gives 5, and the whole array gives 4 − (−1) = 5.

hints: The sum of (max − min) over all subarrays equals (sum of maxima over all subarrays) − (sum of minima over all subarrays). Solve those two separately.
Flip the question for the maxima: for each nums[i], in how many subarrays is it the maximum? That count is (choices for the left end) × (choices for the right end).

A monotonic stack gives, for every index, the nearest bigger value on each side in O(n) total. To avoid counting a subarray twice when values tie, use a strict comparison on one side and a non-strict one on the other.

explain.intuition:
Enumerating subarrays is quadratic however you do it. Instead, ask what each element contributes. nums[i] adds itself once for every subarray where it is the maximum and subtracts itself once for every subarray where it is the minimum. So the answer is Σ nums[i] · (times it is the max − times it is the min).

When is nums[i] the maximum? The subarray must stay between the nearest larger value on the left and the nearest larger value on the right. If those are L and R positions away, there are L · R such subarrays. A stack that keeps values in decreasing order finds both neighbours: when nums[i] pops an index j, then i is j's right boundary and the new stack top is its left boundary. Equal values need a tie rule (pop on ≤), so each subarray is credited to exactly one of its equal maxima.
steps: Write a helper that sums the maximum of every subarray. Keep a stack of indices; walk i from 0 to n, with i = n acting as a value bigger than everything.
While the top j has nums[j] ≤ nums[i]: pop it, let left = j − (new top, or −1) and right = i − j, and add nums[j] · left · right.
Do the same for the minimum with the comparison flipped (pop while nums[j] ≥ nums[i]).
Return the sum of maxima minus the sum of minima.
pitfalls: Using strict comparisons on both sides. With ties like [2, 2, 1, 1] a subarray gets counted for both equal values, and the result is too big.
Forgetting to flush the stack at the end. Elements still on it are maxima up to the end of the array.
Computing only the whole array's max − min and multiplying by the number of subarrays. Each subarray has its own extremes.

solutions.title: Extend from every start
solutions.idea: Fix the left end, extend to the right while updating a running max and min, and add the spread at each step.

solutions.title: Contribution with monotonic stacks
solutions.idea: Sum of all subarray maxima minus sum of all subarray minima. Each value's share is value × left choices × right choices, found when it is popped from a monotonic stack.
